question: A 7-year-old boy has a 3-day history of right otalgia and fever. Otoscopy shows a bulging, erythematous right tympanic membrane. His left ear and neurological examination are normal. What is the most appropriate imaging decision?

answers.text: Obtain HRCT temporal bones immediately to confirm acute otitis media and exclude mastoiditis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Imaging is not indicated for uncomplicated ASOM. The diagnosis is clinical, and HRCT adds no management value while exposing the child to ionising radiation.

answers.text: No imaging — ASOM is a clinical diagnosis; imaging is only indicated if a complication is suspected

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. ASOM is diagnosed clinically by otoscopy (red, bulging, immobile drum). Imaging is reserved for suspected complications: mastoiditis (post-auricular swelling, tenderness), intracranial extension (meningism, altered consciousness), or facial nerve palsy.

answers.text: Plain X-ray of the mastoid (Schuller's view) to look for clouding of the mastoid air cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Plain mastoid X-rays are obsolete in modern ENT practice. HRCT has replaced them for any temporal bone indication. Moreover, imaging is not needed for this uncomplicated ASOM case.

answers.text: MRI brain with gadolinium to exclude intracranial complications before starting antibiotics

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: MRI is appropriate when intracranial complications are suspected (meningism, altered GCS, focal neurology). This child has uncomplicated ASOM with no neurological signs — no imaging is indicated.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall the core rule for ASOM: image only when a complication is suspected — post-auricular swelling (mastoiditis), facial palsy, meningism, or altered consciousness. Uncomplicated ASOM needs no imaging.
Exactly right. The most important principle in ASOM imaging is restraint — it is a clinical diagnosis. Image the complication, not the infection.
